vo_text: Why did Charles Darwin work out how life changes over time
and then lock it in a drawer for 20 years?
By the end of this film you'll know how a few unlabeled birds,
eight years of barnacles and one letter from the other side of the
world forced the biggest secret in biology
into the open.
In the 1830s most naturalists believed every kind
of animal and plant had been made once and never changed.
Saying anything else could ruin a scientist.
But in the summer of 1837 a 28-year-old Charles Darwin drew a little tree
in a private notebook, one kind of animal at the bottom branching into many at the top. Above it he wrote two words, I think. He kept the idea mostly to himself for 20 years.
Then in June 1858 a letter arrived from a collector on the other side of the world.
Inside was Darwin's own theory, worked out by somebody else.
So how did a young man who didn't even label his birds properly stumble onto the secret of how life changes?
When people picture Darwin on
the Galapagos Islands they imagine a flash of genius on the beach. It didn't happen like that.
In 1835 Darwin collected small dark birds there and thought they were a mix of blackbirds, wrens and finches.
For most of them he didn't write down which island they came from.
Even the giant tortoises should have told him. The ship's crew ate them and threw the shells overboard.
Then the island's vice governor Nicholas Lawson mentioned something odd.
He could tell which island a tortoise came from just by the shape of its shell.
Darwin only understood how important that was much later.
Back in London a bird expert called John Gould looked at the skins and gave him a surprise.
They weren't a mix at all. They were all finches.
A group of close cousins each with a differently shaped beak, heavy ones for cracking hard seeds, thin ones for picking at insects and cactus flowers.
Darwin had to borrow labeled birds from his shipmates to work out which beak came from which island
and slowly a question formed.
What if these birds had all come from one kind of finch long ago and changed to fit each island?
That's the tree in the notebook. He could see that one kind of animal could
split into many. But what was doing the shaping?
On the 28th of September
1838 Darwin started reading a book about human populations by Thomas Malthus
and the missing piece fell into place.
Every living thing has far more young than can ever survive. There isn't enough food for all of them so most die young.
Now picture a dry year on one island. Only hard thick seeds are left.
The finches whose beaks happen to be a little deeper can crack them.
They live and they raise chicks with deep beaks like theirs.
Repeat that over thousands of generations and the whole species changes.
Nobody steers it. Nature just keeps the ones that fit. Darwin called it natural selection.
So why didn't he tell the world? He was afraid.
Telling a friend that species could change was, he wrote, like confessing a murder.
And his wife, Emma, was deeply religious.
In 1844 he wrote it all out. About 230 pages sealed it
and left Emma a letter. If he died she was to pay to have it published.
A few months later an unsigned book claiming life
had changed over time was torn apart by scientists.
Then he spent about eight years studying barnacles. So many barnacles the story goes that
one of his children asked a friend where their father did his barnacles.
Darwin's friends kept warning him that if he waited too long someone else would get there first.
Who was that someone?
Alfred Russell Wallace was
not rich like Darwin. He made his living collecting animals and selling them to museums.
In 1852 coming home from four years in the Amazon his ship caught fire and sank.
Almost his whole collection went down with it.
He spent 10 days in an open boat at sea. He went out again anyway.
This times the islands of what is now Indonesia and Malaysia. Over eight years he collected more than 125,000 specimens.
In February 1858 lying ill with a fever Wallace thought about the same book by Malthus
and like Darwin 20 years before he saw it. The ones that fit survive.
Within days he had written it up and he posted it to the one
famous naturalist he knew would be interested. Charles Darwin.
So Darwin could simply hide the letter and keep the credit. Case closed? Wrong.
On the 18th of June 1858 Darwin read Wallace's paper and wrote to his friend Charles Lyle.
All my originality whatever it may amount to will be smashed.
Darwin said he would rather lose the credit than seem to have acted unfairly to Wallace.
Three days later his baby son died of scarlet fever.
His friends found a way out. What happened when the world finally heard?
On the 1st of July 1858
Darwin's friends Charles Lyle and Joseph Hooker had both men's work read out together at the Linnaean Society in London.
Wallace's paper and older writing from Darwin to show he had the idea first.
Neither man was in the room. Darwin was at home grieving for his son.
Wallace hadn't even been asked. He was still in the islands and didn't know for months.
And the reaction? Almost nothing.
The next year the Society's President looked back and said the year had not been marked by any striking discovery.
That pushed Darwin to write. In a little over a year he finished a shorter book for everyone
on the origin of species.
It came out on the 24th of November 1859 and
booksellers had ordered every copy before it even went on sale.
And Wallace? There was no bitter fight.
When he read the book in the islands he praised it and said Darwin had done the work far better than he could.
Years later he even titled his own book about the theory Darwinism.
But one problem worried Darwin for the rest of his life and the answer was already in print.
The problem came from an engineer
called Fleming Jenkin in 1867.
Everyone then thought parents' traits blended in their children like mixing paint.
If that was true one bird with a better beak would have children with a half better beak, then a quarter better. The advantage would wash away before nature could keep it. Darwin never solved it.
But a year earlier in 1866 a friar called Gregor Mendel
had published his work on pea plants.
Traits don't blend like paint. They're passed on whole like beads.
And one more thing. Survival of the fittest wasn't Darwin's phrase.
The writer Herbert Spencer coined it and Darwin only added it to his book later.
Fittest never meant the strongest. It means the one that fits its world best like a key in a lock.
Put Darwin's selection together with Mendel's beads and
you have the core of how biologists explain the living world today.
